scope.name: Southern Islands
notes: Deepens the English Wizards-era Southern Islands mini-set as an 18-card postcard/panorama object.
Covers all 18 modeled rows, split locally into Keiko Fukuyama and Naoyo Kimura artist halves.
Keeps image rights, seller possession, authenticity, condition, price truth, and physical-product collation outside catalog-history authority.

assembly_themes: Southern Islands art reuse boundary for Tropical Present

main_chase_cards.name: Mew
main_chase_cards.why: Mew is the clear collector anchor: iconic, scenic, and mechanically named Rainbow Wave, a perfect thesis card for Southern Islands.

main_chase_cards.name: Slowking
main_chase_cards.why: Slowking carries Johto/movie-era gravity into the tropical half and often attracts character collectors beyond set builders.

main_chase_cards.name: Lapras
main_chase_cards.why: Lapras is an emotional sea-travel anchor for Kimura’s half, strong for collectors who care about atmosphere as much as rarity.

sources.title: Pokemon TCG API v2: Southern Islands set metadata
Bulbapedia: Southern Islands (TCG)

claims.text: The local English WotC catalog records Southern Islands with a July 31, 2001 release date.
Pokemon TCG API-derived local data models Southern Islands as an 18-card mini-set, with 18 rows returned for set.id si1.
The local release classifies Southern Islands as a mini_set rather than a booster expansion or deck.
The local credited-artist surface splits the set evenly: Keiko Fukuyama is credited on cards 1-9 and Naoyo Kimura on cards 10-18.
Southern Islands matters because it is a scenic object first: an English WotC-era mini-set where cards behave like fragments of a postcard panorama rather than only game pieces.

Agents should identify Southern Islands by English WotC set id si1, card number 1-18, artist half, and scene/postcard context, while separating it from Japanese Southern Islands, Tropical Present art reuse, and ordinary character-name matches.

special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, seller story, or agent result says Southern Islands, si1, Rainbow Island, Tropical Island, postcard, Mew Southern Islands, Keiko Fukuyama, Naoyo Kimura, Tropical Present, Japanese Southern Islands, or WotC mini-set.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Confirm the English WotC Southern Islands route and card number before treating a scan or listing as this mini-set.
steps: Confirm English WotC Southern Islands / set.id si1 rather than Japanese Southern Islands, Tropical Present, or generic tropical-themed promos.
Confirm the card number is one of 1-18 and matches the claimed character.
Use the artist split as a sanity check: cards 1-9 are Keiko Fukuyama in the local data, cards 10-18 are Naoyo Kimura.
Treat Mew as the collector anchor, not as a price guarantee.
Separate Southern Islands set cards from Fan Club Tropical Present objects that reuse Southern Islands sea-scene memory.
Use API/provider images as reference witnesses only; they are not seller evidence or approved display/training rights.
Before trade/spendability use, require seller-controlled front/back photos, title/name, set symbol/number area, copyright/artist area, surface/corners, and any slab/cert evidence.
Do not infer authenticity, condition, possession, or complete product packaging from the catalog row alone.

narrative.human_title: Southern Islands — the set as postcard weather
narrative.why_it_matters: Southern Islands is one of the clearest examples of Pokemon cards becoming an illustrated place. Mew gives the set its obvious gravity, but the deeper joy is the assembly: eighteen small windows, two artists, two island moods, and a WotC-era product that feels closer to a travel keepsake than a normal expansion. It is exactly the kind of set an agent should understand as culture, not just inventory.
